items.prompt: State what is meant by the term international migration.
items.canonical_answer: A move to live in another country, crossing a national border, as when someone leaves Mexico to live and work in the United States.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - a permanent or long-term move across a national border to live; a holiday or a day trip is not migration.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why people migrate from rural areas to cities.
items.canonical_answer: The countryside pushes people out because farm work is seasonal and poorly paid, and schools and clinics are thin on the ground. The city pulls them in because jobs are more numerous and better paid, and services are closer. Because families expect to do better there, the move is usually driven by both sides at once, a reason to leave and a place worth going to.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: a push factor of the origin (pay, work, services), which drives people away; a pull factor of the destination (jobs, services, pay); so both together cause the move, because migration needs a reason to leave and a place to go.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
A survey asks 200 migrants arriving in Windhoek where they came from:

| origin | farm in the same region | town in the same region | another region of Namibia | outside Namibia |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| number of people | 118 | 46 | 28 | 8 |

Describe what the table shows about where the migrants came from.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows most arrivals coming from nearby: 118 of the 200, more than half, left farms in the same region, and another 46 came from towns in it, so 164 of the 200 moved within their own region. Only 28 came from other regions of Namibia and just 8 from outside the country. The pattern shown is a short-distance, internal move from the land to the capital, which fits the idea that distance and cost filter who moves.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - most migrants come from close by, within the same region (1 mark).
Values: the figures with their numbers, 118 of 200 from farms and 164 of 200 within the region (1 mark); the small shares from far away, 28 and 8, so the figures support the words (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A survey finds that most international migrants from a poor district cross into the neighbouring country, though wages are higher in a rich country further away. Suggest why most choose the neighbouring country.
items.canonical_answer: The neighbouring country is closer, so the journey costs less and needs less time, which matters where savings are small. Crossing one border instead of two needs fewer papers and less risk, because the resource here says the district is poor and the rich country is far. And because relatives often settle first in the nearest place with work, the newcomer has family to help there, which suggests why the stream follows the cheap, short route.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used - the district is poor, so travel cost matters, and the nearer country is the affordable move (1 mark).
Reasons: fewer borders and fewer papers on the short route (1 mark); so family networks and cost send most movers to the nearest labour market, not the richest one (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner labels a family's move from Oshakati to Windhoek "an international migration". Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The move crosses no national border, so it is internal migration, movement within one country. International migration is a move to live in another country. The test is whether the move crosses a national border: Oshakati to Windhoek stays inside Namibia, so it cannot be international.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the move is internal, because it stays within Namibia and is not the same as crossing a border.
1 mark: the correct idea - international migration means a move to live in another country.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Asked for the pull factors attracting migrants to a city, a learner writes: "The farms are failing and there is no work at home." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has listed push factors, things about the origin that drive people away, when the question asks for pull factors, things about the destination that attract. Failing farms and no work are about the place left, not the place chosen. The test is whether the factor is about the place left or the place chosen.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - push factors of the origin given instead of pull factors, which is not the same thing.
1 mark: the correct idea - pull factors belong to the destination, such as jobs, pay and services there.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two benefits migration brings to a destination.
items.canonical_answer: Migrants fill jobs, including the work local people often avoid, which means harvests are picked and building sites run at full strength. Their spending and taxes support the local economy and services, because new workers rent rooms, buy food and pay into the system their children then use.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per benefit, 2 in all: workers fill labour shortages; spending and taxes support the economy and services.
Each benefit is taken to its consequence, because or so or which means.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two problems rapid migration can cause for a destination.
items.canonical_answer: Housing and services strain before they can grow, because schools and clinics are built for the old population size, so classes swell and waiting lists lengthen. Rapid arrivals can stir resentment, because newcomers get blamed for crowding and rents, which makes the city harder for everyone to live in.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per problem, 2 in all: services over capacity; resentment and housing pressure.
Each problem is taken to its consequence, because or so or which means.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how the departure of young adults changes the villages they leave behind.
items.canonical_answer: The loss of working-age adults causes a shortage of labour on the land, so harvests shrink and some fields fall out of use. Fewer carers remain for the old, so grandparents raise children alone, which leads to strain on the households left. The chain ends with remittances offsetting some of the loss, because the money sent home builds houses and pays fees, so the effect is a mixture of loss and support.
marking_guidance: Cause: young adults leave, which starts the chain (1 mark).
So: the land loses workers and the old lose carers, which means production and care both fall (1 mark).
Effect: remittances partly offset the loss, so the final impact on the village is both thinner and better funded.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
A region's records show, for the years 2000 and 2020:

| measure | 2000 | 2020 |
|---|---|---|
| people aged 20-34 living there | 48 000 | 27 000 |
| money received from migrants abroad / N$ million | 3 | 96 |
| houses built or improved | 210 | 2 640 |

Describe what the table shows about the impact of migration on this region.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the region losing its young adults and being paid for it. Residents aged 20-34 fell from 48 000 to 27 000, a loss of 21 000 people, while money from migrants abroad rose from N$3 million to N$96 million, thirty-two times the 2000 figure. The houses built or improved rose from 210 to 2 640, so the pattern shown is a thinner young population funding a building boom from abroad.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - young adults leave, money arriving rises steeply (1 mark).

Values: the paired figures with units, 48 000 down to 27 000 and N$3 million up to N$96 million (1 mark); the housing figure used to show what the money does, so the figures support the words (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A migrant mother works long hours in a city job, sends money home each month and has brought her two children to the city school. Suggest two gains and one cost of the move for her family.
items.canonical_answer: The gains suggested by this example are the higher pay, which pays for the children's schooling and the money sent home, and the city school and clinics, which serve the children better than the origin could. The cost is the separation and the strain: long hours mean the children see little of her, so the family trades time together for the income.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used - the pay, the remittances and the school place are read from the situation given (1 mark).
Reasons: the two gains each carried to its consequence (1 mark); the cost named with its consequence, so the answer balances rather than lists (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Asked "Describe the impacts of migration on the destination", a learner writes about the homesickness of the migrants and the poverty they left. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The question asks about the destination, the place joined, but the learner has answered for the migrants and the origin. Those are different sides of migration: the destination's impacts are jobs filled, services strained, rents and resentment. The test is whose side the question asks about.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the answer is on the wrong side, migrants and origin instead of the destination, which is not the same thing.
1 mark: the correct idea - destination impacts such as filled jobs and strained services.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: For the migration from Mexico to the United States, describe two features of the stream.
items.canonical_answer: It is one of the largest international streams in the world, with more than a million people a year crossing, mostly at the border cities. The money the migrants send home reaches about 60 billion United States dollars a year (early 2020s), among the biggest remittance flows anywhere.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the size of the annual flow; the remittance figure with its year.
Each fact is a feature of the named stream, Mexico to the United States, not a general point about migration.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: For Mexico and the United States, explain why the migration stream has run for decades and what it does to the villages that lose people.
items.canonical_answer: The stream runs because the wage gap between the two countries has lasted: a worker earns several times more north of the border, so the pull stays strong year after year. Family networks in states such as California and Texas settle each newcomer into a job and a room, which means every migrant makes the next one's move easier, so the stream renews itself. In the villages that lose people, working-age adults are gone, so the land is farmed less. But the remittances they send, about 60 billion United States dollars a year nationally in the early 2020s, build houses and keep children in school, so the villages lose labour and gain money at once.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 4, each point using the named example: the wage gap persists, so the pull lasts; family networks lower the cost of moving, so the stream renews; the villages lose labour, so land is farmed less; remittances arrive, so houses and schooling are paid for from abroad.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: For a named international migration, explain the causes of the migration and its impacts on the country the migrants leave. [7]
items.canonical_answer: The migration from Mexico to the United States moves more than a million people a year, most of them crossing at the border cities to work in farming, construction and services. The causes are a wage gap that has lasted decades: farm work in parts of Mexico pays a fraction of United States wages, so a worker can earn several times more north of the border, and family networks in states such as California and Texas settle newcomers into jobs and rooms, so each migrant makes the next one's move cheaper and safer. For Mexico, the stream empties villages of working-age adults, so some land is farmed less and grandparents raise children alone. The money the migrants send home, about 60 billion United States dollars a year in the early 2020s, among the largest flows in the world, builds houses and keeps children in school, so the country loses labour and gains a steady income at once. The impacts on the place left are therefore mixed: thinner villages, better funded.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about migration in general, with no named example or only general points about push and pull.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named migration, capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - Mexico, the United States, the border cities, California and Texas, the remittance figure with its year - covering both causes and impacts on the origin.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows a migration survey of one district:

| year | working-age adults living in the district | remittances received / N$ million | farms fully worked |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1995 | 32 400 | 0.4 | 1 480 |
| 2010 | 24 100 | 27 | 1 210 |
| 2025 | 19 800 | 83 | 940 |

(a) Identify the measure that increased over the whole period. [1]
(b) Describe the change in the district's working-age population between 1995 and 2025. [2]
(c) Suggest how the remittances changed life for the families who stayed. [3]
(d) Suggest one reason why fewer farms are fully worked. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Remittances received.
(b) Working-age adults fell from 32 400 to 19 800, a loss of 12 600 people, or about 39 per cent of the 1995 total, and the fall continued in both halves of the period.
(c) The money from abroad suggests the families can build or improve houses, as in the districts where remittances fund construction, and pay school fees rather than taking children out of school to work. Because N$83 million a year reaches the district, the money from one worker abroad can exceed what several could earn at home, so the families who stayed gained income even as they lost members. Some of it goes on daily needs too, so the remittances replace lost local earnings.
(d) The working-age adults who would farm them have left, so there are not enough hands to work every field fully.
marking_guidance: Resource: (a) read from the table - remittances is the only rising measure - 1 mark.
Figures: (b) 2 marks - the fall stated with the paired figures and the size of the loss.
Marks and reasons: (c) 3 marks - two or three uses of the remittances carried to their consequences with the resource's figures; (d) 2 marks - the labour shortage linked to the departures.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.2 claim ledger.
